gap: No result ChatGPT got states that an average US driver's day (13,735 mi/yr ÷ 365 = 37.6 mi) uses about 10.2 kWh from the wall in a 2026 Model Y Long Range AWD. That refills in about 1.8 hours at 24 A and 2.6 hours at 16 A. None of them states that a 40 A charger costs $60.76 per kW it can actually deliver on a 30 A dryer circuit, against $41.66/kW for the EVDANCE 24 A unit.
standout_why: I compared against plugandrange.com/portable-chargers/nema-14-30, thechargecurve.com/home-ev-chargers/best-nema-14-30 and intrysys.com/.../charge-ev-from-dryer-outlet. All three already give 5.76 kW, about 15–20 mi of range per hour, and per-night totals (8 h ≈ 46 kWh, 10 h ≈ 58 kWh, about 200 mi). Plug & Range also says 16 A gives 'over 130 miles across ten hours'. None of them works out how many hours a typical day's driving takes from a sourced national average, what that costs at the EIA residential rate, or what each charger costs per kW it can deliver on a 30 A circuit. Plug & Range and The Charge Curve both recommend the 40 A Grizzl-E Mini at $349.99 without pointing out that on a dryer outlet it runs at the same 24 A as a $240 unit.
decides: This supports a 24 A charger with a 14-30 plug (EVDANCE) as the value pick and argues against paying for a 40 A unit that has to be set to 24 A. It also shows the 24 A vs 16 A difference matters only to drivers who cover well over the average in a short overnight window: 37.6 mi/day takes 1.8 h at 24 A and 2.6 h at 16 A, both far inside an 8–10 h night. For an average commuter, the $129.99 VEVOR 16 A unit, at $33.85 per usable kW, is enough if it has the right plug. Its NEMA 10-30 plug fits only 3-prong outlets.
